Casino War Basics: Bet Structure, the Tie Rule, and the Real House Edge

Published October 5, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Casino War takes the simplest possible children's card game — whoever has the higher card wins — and turns it into a casino table game by adding exactly one decision point: what to do when you tie. That single rule is the entire strategic content of the game, and it's worth understanding precisely, because getting it wrong is the difference between a perfectly reasonable 2.9% house edge and a much worse one you accidentally chose for yourself.

In this guide

  1. How a hand of Casino War is dealt
  2. The tie rule: surrender, go to war, or bonus side bet

How a hand of Casino War is dealt

You place a bet, the dealer deals you one card face up and deals one card face up to themselves. Aces are high. Whichever card is higher wins; a winning player bet pays even money (1:1). There are no additional cards, no hitting, no splitting, and nothing resembling a strategic decision in the normal run of the game. If your card beats the dealer's, you win your bet back plus an equal amount. If the dealer's card beats yours, you lose your bet. The entire game, in the overwhelming majority of hands, resolves in about ten seconds with a single comparison of two cards.

Most tables use six standard 52-card decks shuffled together, which matters slightly for the probability of ties (discussed below) but doesn't change the basic win/lose mechanics. Some online and live-dealer versions use a different number of decks; always check the table's rules before you sit down, since deck count has a small but real effect on the numbers in this guide.

The tie rule: surrender, go to war, or bonus side bet

A tie — both you and the dealer drawing the same rank — happens roughly once every 20 to 21 hands with a six-deck shoe, more often than most new players expect. When it happens, you get a choice:

OptionWhat happens
SurrenderForfeit half your original bet and the hand ends immediately.
Go to warPlace an additional bet equal to your original wager. The dealer burns three cards, then deals one new card each to you and the dealer. If you win this second comparison, you're paid even money on the "war" bet only, and your original bet is returned as a push. If you lose, you lose both bets. Most casinos also pay a small bonus — commonly 1:1 on just the original wager in addition — if you win the war with a tied rank again, though exact bonus rules vary by casino.
Bonus side bet (Tie)A separate optional wager, placed before the cards are dealt, that pays out specifically when the initial two cards tie. Covered on its own below — it's a different bet with a much worse edge.

Surrendering guarantees you lose exactly half your stake every time a tie occurs. Going to war means risking an additional, equal-sized bet for a chance to either push (get your original stake back) or lose both bets. There's no secret third option and no situational read that should change your choice hand to hand — one of these two is simply the better mathematical decision every single time a tie occurs, which is the next section.

The math behind "going to war" every time

Surrendering on a tie costs you exactly half your original bet, guaranteed, with certainty, no variance. Going to war costs you nothing extra if you lose outright (you were already going to lose your original bet's worth either way on a true loss, roughly), but let's work the actual comparison properly: once a tie occurs and you decide to go to war, the new one-card draw between you and the dealer is close to — not exactly, but close to — a coin flip, since you're drawing from a reduced shoe with three cards burned and your tied rank partially used up. Because ties push the original bet back and only decide the new "war" wager, going to war has a noticeably better expected cost than automatically forfeiking half your stake via surrender.

Put concretely: surrendering loses you 0.5 units with 100% certainty every time a tie happens. Going to war, you'll lose 2 units (original plus war bet) a little under half the time, and push the original bet back while winning 1 unit on the war bet a little more than half the time once you account for the removed cards slightly favoring the player in a tie-rematch scenario. Run through the full math and going to war comes out ahead of surrendering by a real, if modest, margin over the long run. This is one of the very few genuinely "always do this" rules in casino gambling — unlike blackjack basic strategy, which branches by hand, Casino War's entire strategy chart is one line: always go to war on a tie, never surrender.

Takeaway: The only decision in Casino War that matters is what you do on a tie, and the answer is always the same: go to war. Surrendering sounds like the "safe" choice, but it locks in a guaranteed loss that going to war beats on average.

Where the real house edge comes from

With correct play (always going to war, never surrendering), Casino War carries a house edge of roughly 2.88% on the original bet — a touch higher than American roulette and noticeably higher than blackjack or baccarat, but still well within the range of a mainstream, low-complexity table game. That edge comes almost entirely from the asymmetric payout structure on ties: when you go to war and win, you're only paid even money on the additional war wager, while your original bet merely pushes rather than also paying out at even money. If a tied war-win paid even money on both the original and war bets, the game would be far closer to even, maybe even in the player's favor; the casino's margin lives specifically in that asymmetry.

If you surrender on every tie instead of going to war, the house edge roughly doubles, landing closer to 3.7%, depending on the exact ruleset and deck count. That's the entire cost of picking the "wrong" option in the game's one and only decision point, and it's a useful reminder that even a game this simple can carry meaningfully different real-world odds depending on one choice most players make without thinking about it.

The standalone Tie bet: a different, much worse game

Separate from the surrender-or-war decision after a tie occurs, most Casino War tables also offer an optional side bet, placed before any cards are dealt, that simply wins if the initial two cards tie. This bet usually pays somewhere around 10:1 at physical casinos, though online and live-dealer versions vary. Because ties only happen roughly once every 20 hands with a six-deck shoe, true odds would require a payout closer to 20:1 (adjusted slightly for the exact tie probability) for the bet to be fair. A 10:1 payout against those odds gives the house an edge on this side bet in the roughly 15-18% range at most tables — several times worse than the base game, and worse than nearly any other common side bet across other table games covered elsewhere on this site. Treat the Tie side bet as a novelty, not a strategy.

How it stacks up against other simple table games

GameTypical house edgeDecisions required
Casino War (correct play)~2.88%One: always go to war on a tie
Baccarat (banker bet)~1.06%None — fixed drawing rules
Blackjack (basic strategy)~0.5%Many, hand by hand
American roulette (even-money bets)~5.26%None
Casino War (surrender every tie)~3.7%One: the wrong one

What makes Casino War distinctive on that list isn't the edge itself — plenty of games sit in the same 2-3% neighborhood — it's the ratio of decisions to edge. You get a house edge competitive with baccarat for a game that requires zero card-counting, zero strategy charts, and exactly one rule to memorize. For players who want a low-complexity table game without learning a full strategy chart, that combination is the actual appeal, more than the specific number itself.

Common mistakes new players make

The single biggest mistake is surrendering on ties out of a vague instinct that "going to war" means risking more money unnecessarily — it does mean risking more money, but the expected cost of doing so is lower than the guaranteed cost of surrendering, which is exactly why correct strategy says to do it every time. The second common mistake is treating the Tie side bet as a reasonable way to add excitement; it's a sucker bet by the standards of this game specifically, carrying several times the house edge of the base wager for a payout that doesn't come close to compensating for the real odds. If you want a broader sense of how this game's edge compares across the full range of table games, our house edge guide covers the landscape, and if you're deciding how much of your bankroll to allocate to a lower-complexity game like this one, see our casino bankroll management guide.

Frequently asked questions

Should I surrender or go to war when I tie with the dealer?

Always go to war. Surrendering locks in a guaranteed loss of half your bet, while going to war has a better expected cost even though it occasionally means losing both bets outright.

What is the house edge on Casino War?

Roughly 2.88% with correct play (always going to war). If you surrender every tie instead, the effective house edge roughly doubles to around 3.7%.

Is the Tie side bet worth playing?

No. It typically carries a house edge in the 15-18% range at common payout odds, far worse than the base game, because the payout doesn't match how often a tie actually occurs.

How often do ties actually happen in Casino War?

With a standard six-deck shoe, a tie happens roughly once every 20 to 21 hands, which is more frequently than most new players assume.

Does the number of decks used change the odds?

Yes, slightly. Deck count affects the exact probability of ties and the precise edge, though the "always go to war" rule stays correct regardless of how many decks a specific table uses.
